title: Powers of Two Form a Distinct Subset Sum Set
description: Proves that the set {2⁰, 2¹, ..., 2^{n-1}} has distinct subset sums for every n, using binary representation uniqueness. Provides the existence theorem needed to make the minimum DSS bound function well-defined in the Erdős #1 formalization.

meta.author: Lean Genius Researcher, 2026
meta.assumptions: None. All theorems proved from first principles using Mathlib's Finset API and strong induction.

pow2_sum_inj: subsets of {0,...,n-1} with equal power-of-2 sums are identical (binary uniqueness)
powersOfTwo_hasDistinctSubsetSums: {2^i : i < n} has distinct subset sums
dss_existence: for all n, ∃ A with |A|=n, all(a ≤ n·2^n), and DSS(A)

overview.historicalContext:
**Erdős Problem #1** asks for the minimum $N$ such that some $n$-element subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has all $2^n$ subset sums distinct. Before bounding $N$ from below or above, one must know such sets exist at all. The powers of two $\{1, 2, 4, \ldots, 2^{n-1}\}$ provide the canonical existence witness: each natural number has a unique binary representation, so no two distinct subsets can share the same sum.

This existence result is foundational for the formalization: the Lean definition of `minDSSBound(n)` (the minimum $N$) uses `Nat.find`, which requires an explicit witness to justify well-definedness. The file `Erdos1OQ03.lean` (Conway-Guy construction) references this existence theorem as its `Nat.find` input.
overview.problemStatement: For each $n \geq 0$, prove that the $n$-element set $A = \{2^0, 2^1, \ldots, 2^{n-1}\}$ has distinct subset sums — that is, no two distinct subsets of $A$ have the same sum.
overview.text: A 187-line formalization proving that powers of two form a distinct subset sum set for every n. The proof is in three parts: (I) auxiliary lemmas establishing the geometric sum identity and the bound on subset sums of index sets; (II) the main binary uniqueness theorem, proved by strong induction; and (III) the existence theorem providing an n-element DSS set bounded by n·2^n, which fills the sorry in Erdos1OQ03.lean.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Part I** establishes two key lemmas by induction. `geom_sum_pow2` proves ∑_{i<n} 2^i + 1 = 2^n by induction on n. `sum_pow2_lt_of_subset_range` uses monotonicity of sums to bound any subset sum.

**Part II** proves binary uniqueness (`pow2_sum_inj`) by strong induction on n. Given S, T ⊆ {0,...,n-1} with equal power-of-2 sums, there are four cases for membership of n-1: (a) both contain n-1: erase it from both sides (the 2^{n-1} contributions cancel) and apply IH; (b/c) exactly one contains n-1: the subset containing n-1 contributes ≥ 2^{n-1} to the sum, while the other contributes < 2^{n-1} by Part I — contradiction; (d) neither contains n-1: restrict to range n-1 and apply IH directly.

**Part III** applies the preimage technique: given S, T ⊆ {2^i : i < n} with equal sums, define index sets S' = {i < n : 2^i ∈ S} and T' = {i < n : 2^i ∈ T}. By `Finset.sum_image`, S.sum id = S'.sum (2^·). The equality S.sum id = T.sum id then gives S'.sum (2^·) = T'.sum (2^·), so binary uniqueness gives S' = T', hence S = T.
keyInsights: **Binary representation uniqueness**: equal power-of-2 sums imply equal index sets — the core mathematical fact, corresponding to uniqueness of binary representations
**Strong induction structure**: the four-case split (both/one/neither contain n-1) exactly mirrors the key step in uniqueness of binary representation proofs

**Preimage trick**: reducing from sums over values (S.sum id) to sums over indices (S'.sum (2^·)) via Finset.sum_image is the key bridge between the abstract DSS property and the index-level induction
**Sum bound**: sum_pow2_lt_of_subset_range gives 'any proper subset of {0,...,n-1} has power-of-2 sum < 2^n', which is the quantitative tool that rules out the cross-cases (b/c) in the induction
**n·2^n bound**: each 2^i for i < n satisfies 2^i < 2^n ≤ n·2^n (using Nat.le_mul_of_pos_left), giving a clean polynomial-times-exponential bound without case analysis on n=0

**Nat.find well-definedness**: dss_existence provides the existential witness required for Nat.find to produce a well-typed noncomputable definition of minDSSBound — without this theorem, Erdos1OQ03.lean could not define minDSSBound at all

**Gap between existence and optimality**: the n·2^n existence bound is far from optimal — the Conway-Guy sequence achieves max element ≈ 0.22·2^n and the Erdős #1 conjecture asks whether c·2^n/√n is the true threshold; formalizing existence is the prerequisite for studying tightness

sections.title: Auxiliary Lemmas for Binary Injectivity
sections.summary: Three supporting lemmas: geometric sum identity, subset sum bound, and binary representation uniqueness by strong induction.
sections.mathContext: $\sum_{i<n} 2^i + 1 = 2^n$; any $S \subseteq \{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ has $\sum_{i \in S} 2^i < 2^n$; $S, T \subseteq \{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, $\sum_S 2^i = \sum_T 2^i \Rightarrow S = T$

sections.title: The DSS Property of Powers of Two
sections.summary: Proves that {2^i : i < n} has distinct subset sums using the preimage index trick and binary uniqueness.
sections.mathContext: $\forall S, T \subseteq \{2^0,\ldots,2^{n-1}\},\ \sum S = \sum T \Rightarrow S = T$

sections.title: Existence of n-Element DSS Sets (Main Theorem)
sections.summary: For any n, constructs an n-element set with all elements ≤ n·2^n and distinct subset sums. Used as Nat.find witness in minDSSBound.
sections.mathContext: $\forall n,\ \exists A,\ |A|=n \wedge (\forall a \in A,\ a \leq n \cdot 2^n) \wedge \text{DSS}(A)$

crossReferences.description: Provides the foundational existence result for Erdős Problem #1: proves DSS sets of every size exist
dss_existence fills the sorry in minDSSBound (Nat.find witness), making the minimum DSS bound function well-defined

conclusion.summary: Fully verified: {2^i : i < n} has distinct subset sums for every n, and n-element DSS sets exist with all elements bounded by n·2^n. Zero sorries, zero axioms.
conclusion.implications: This existence theorem closes the gap in Erdos1OQ03.lean, making minDSSBound a well-defined noncomputable function. It also serves as a standalone verified formalization of binary representation uniqueness in the Finset setting.
openQuestions: Can the bound n·2^n be tightened? The Conway-Guy sequence achieves max element ~0.22·2^n, far smaller than n·2^n.
Can the binary uniqueness proof be generalized to other bases, giving existence for sets with k-ary representation uniqueness?
Is there a direct Lean proof that the powers-of-two set is the unique (up to scaling) set achieving the counting bound 2^n ≤ n·N + 1 with equality?

mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ n, ∃ A : Finset ℕ, A.card = n ∧ (∀ a ∈ A, a ≤ n * 2 ^ n) ∧ hasDistinctSubsetSums A
